newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week-Low inflation data to support.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week-Low inflation data to support.

text.p: British gilts are set to enjoy a week of steady gains with the little data on offer likely to prove supportive, dealers said.
The market got off to a good start on Monday after Bank of England Governor Eddie George said underlying inflation would fall to the government's target of 2.5 percent this year.

Speaking to reporters at the Bank for International Settlements in Basle, Switzerland, he questioned whether it could stay there, but most market participants took that as the final nail in the coffin of a pre-election rate rise.
Prime Minister John Major is expected to call an election for May 1. Underlying retail price inflation was 3.1 percent year-on-year in January.
"It looks like George is pedalling backwards fairly quickly," said Steve Scott, gilts analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
Nonetheless, longer-dated gilts were most likely to star this week, he said, even though the receding chance of a near-term increase in six percent base rates will support the short end.
"The steepening we had last week was probably a bit overdone. As the market moves higher, we should see the long end outperform," Scott said.
In terms of economic data, producer price figures released earlier on Monday proved no problem for the market.
Output prices were up just 1.3 percent year-on-year in February, the lowest rate of increase since October 1986, and input prices fell 6.6 percent on the year.
The March gilt future shot up to 111-30 and Stuart Frost, market analyst at NatWest Markets, said it would go further in the days ahead.
"The market expected some pretty good figures but the June gilt contract could recover towards 112-16 this week," he said.

He added that the June short sterling future would head for 93.70. It was trading at 93.62 by 1000 GMT on Monday, already pricing in no more than a 25 basis point rise in base rates in the first half of the year. "Everything points towards a very low interest rate environment irrespective of whether we've got an election or not," Frost said.

On Wednesday, industrial production figures for January will be released. Manufacturing output is forecast up 0.3 percent on the month, according to a Reuter poll of economists, as buoyant domestic demand offsets weak export markets.
But that sort of figure will set off no inflationary alarms in the gilt market, as the super-strong pound continues to dog British exporters.

"Weaker export demand has yet to fully impact upon the sector and, on our forecasts, will continue to be partly offset by the strength of domestic orders," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
But in spite of a benign set of figures this week, outperformance could be a tall order for the gilt market.
"As soon as (the yield spread to Bunds) gets into the 160s it becomes more difficult to make progress but logic suggests we should continue," Scott said.
He set a target for the gilt/Bund spread of 165 basis points but doubted that it would be met in the next five days. Early on Monday, the spread stood at 172 basis points.

In terms of curve plays, Peter Warburton at Williams de Broe advised buying the 8.0 percent gilt due 2003 and switching out of the 7.0 percents of 2002. The seven-year stock currently yields 16 basis points more than the six-year.
